title: The Portrait That Keeps Getting Satie's Heartbreak Wrong
standfirst: In 1894 Santiago Rusiñol painted the composer Erik Satie at a piano with a young Parisian model, a year after the only love affair Satie ever had ended in devastation. Some recent readings assume the woman in the room is that lost love. She isn't — and the painting's own details argue that everyone present knew exactly what they were staging.

sections.heading: The Candle That Isn't Lit
sections.body:
On the edge of the piano in Rusiñol's canvas sits a candle holder, swiveled forward as though caught mid-use — except no candle burns in it, and its real function seems to be keeping the two figures at a proper distance rather than lighting anything. The young woman at the keys studies her score with a stare that gives away nothing. The man beside her has his eyes closed; he could be listening, or could be somewhere else entirely. Rusiñol's loose brushwork catches just enough light through his pince-nez that the closed eyes read as almost awake. None of it is scenery. It's an argument built out of props.

The man is the composer Erik Satie, painted by his friend Santiago Rusiñol in Paris in 1894 and portrayed four times altogether across Rusiñol's work. The [painting's own account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Romance_%28Rusi%C3%B1ol%29), of the copy now held at the Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya in Barcelona, says this ordinary-looking domestic scene has acquired real notoriety in Satie's iconography in the 21st century — not for what it shows, but for who people now assume the woman is.

sections.heading: The One Love He Actually Had
sections.body:
A year before Rusiñol picked up his brush, Satie had [the only intimate relationship of his life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Satie), with the painter Suzanne Valadon — a woman Rusiñol also knew personally, having befriended her himself during his Montmartre years. Valadon moved into a room beside Satie's at rue Cortot; he proposed marriage after their first night together, gave her the nickname "Biqui," and wrote her passionate notes about her hands, her eyes, her feet. He composed a set of pieces, the Danses gothiques, specifically to calm himself while it lasted. After a few months she left. Satie described what remained as "nothing but an icy loneliness that fills the head with emptiness and the heart with sadness." He never had another relationship of the kind.

That history is documented well enough that some recent commentary on this painting — citing the musicologist Caroline Potter's study of Satie — has assumed A Romance must be exactly this: an idealised record of Satie and Valadon together at the piano, painted by a mutual friend. It's a reasonable guess. It's also wrong.

sections.heading: How to Tell She Isn't in It
sections.body:
The woman in the painting is Stéphanie Nantas, the daughter of a music teacher, who had become Rusiñol's favourite Paris model that same year and turns up in roughly a dozen of his other canvases from the period, under titles like Melancholy and Reverie — always with the same tall, fragile look and haunted eyes that the Valadon theory has to explain away. The timing doesn't help the theory either: by 1894, Valadon's affair with Satie was already a year in the past, and Rusiñol's [other paintings of Nantas from this period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Romance_%28Rusi%C3%B1ol%29) identify her clearly enough on their own.

Rusiñol supplies his own rebuttal, painted the same year. The Laughing Girl (1894) shows an unnamed young woman with Valadon's big blue eyes, her favourite dark red hairstyle, and something of her cheek in the pose — a genuine likeness, in a picture that isn't A Romance. Rusiñol painted Valadon when he meant to paint Valadon, and painted Nantas here. He doesn't seem to have taken sides when Valadon left Satie; he stayed close enough to both to paint them separately, in the same year, without confusing one for the other.

sections.heading: The Muse Who Outlasted the Painting
sections.body:
Nantas herself is a thinner record than either of the two men painted around her. She posed not only for Rusiñol but for Pierre Puvis de Chavannes, Ramon Casas and Alfredo Müller, and in several surviving portraits she wears deuil noire — mourning black — for a loss nobody has identified; she never married. Rusiñol's own portraits of her ran darker than this one: La medalla and La morfina, a before-and-after pair showing a woman using morphine, painted at a time when Rusiñol himself was addicted to the drug, though nothing in the record suggests Nantas was.

She and Satie stayed in each other's lives long after the sitting. In 1901 he [dedicated a piano waltz, Poudre d'or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Romance_%28Rusi%C3%B1ol%29), to her. In 1908 the two of them stood as witnesses at Alfredo Müller's wedding, signing the certificate side by side. By then she had been, since 1896, the companion of the Italian painter Egisto Fabbri; his 1910 portrait of her shows a woman still elegant but visibly marked by the tuberculosis that would kill her in 1913. Whatever heartbreak sits inside this painting, the woman who actually posed for it stayed close to Satie for two more decades — on paper, if nowhere else.

sections.heading: Filed as Impressionism, Staged Like a Joke
sections.body:
The corpus here files A Romance under Impressionism, the movement's usual catch-all for a scene like this. It fits awkwardly. What Rusiñol brought back from his years in Paris was less Impressionism's interest in observed light than the psychological weight of [Franco-Belgian Symbolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Rusi%C3%B1ol), and this canvas is built around psychology, not weather. The empty candle, the unreadable stare, the too-perfect domesticity — those are a Symbolist's props, not an Impressionist's.

There's a further irony sitting in the room itself. Rusiñol had spent years mailing dispatches from bohemian Montmartre to the Spanish paper La Vanguardia, dispatches he later admitted were a pose struck for the writing. By 1894 he was renting a genuinely luxurious flat on the Île Saint-Louis — its jade-green walls are visible in this very canvas — and using it to paint two real Montmartre bohemians performing a respectable, candlelit courtship that neither of them was actually having. One account of the picture calls this, in effect, a private joke, and raises the possibility that Satie — a man who managed his own image obsessively — suggested the idea for the painting himself. If that's right, nobody in this room was quite where the title says they were: not the couple, not the romance, and, according to the corpus, not even the movement.
